The words

Lord! deliver; Thou canst save;
Save from evil, Mighty God!
Hear — oh! hear the kneeling slave;
Break — oh! break th' oppressor's rod.

May the captive's pleading fill
All the earth, and all the sky;
Every other voice be still,
While he pleads with God on high.

He, whose ear is everywhere,
Who doth silent sorrow see,
Will regard the captive's prayer,
Will from bondage set him free.

From the tyranny within,
Save Thy children, Lord! we pray;
Chains of iron, chains of sin,
Cast, forever cast away.

Love to man, and love to God,
Are the weapons of our war;
These can break th' oppressor's rod —
Burst the bonds that we abhor.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Ab and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (A♭).
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Eliza Lee Cabot Follen wrote these words. They were printed in the supplement of the 1866 edition of A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1866), as hymn 581, “Prayer for the Slave”.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Sevens (7.7.7.7), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to ST. BEES; any other Sevens tune fits them as well.

  • Words: Eliza Lee Cabot Follen (1787–1860)
  • Music (1862): John Bacchus Dykes (1823–1876)

Tune ST. BEES by John Bacchus Dykes (1823–1876); words by Eliza Lee Cabot Follen (1787–1860).

Questions about Lord! Deliver; Thou Canst Save

What is the doh of Lord! Deliver; Thou Canst Save?

In this version, in Ab major, doh is Ab. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Lord! Deliver; Thou Canst Save start on?

It starts on d (A♭ in Ab major). Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is Lord! Deliver; Thou Canst Save in the public domain?

Yes. Eliza Lee Cabot Follen died in 1860, John Bacchus Dykes died in 1876; the words were in print by 1866 and the music in 1862. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
